p6c5.essay:
The chapter opens with two men 'measuring their strength' on a pavement and ends with a woman measuring the distance across a room with a revolver. In between Dostoevsky does something close to stage farce, the rattling tour of the staircase, the bureau, the cab, all in Svidrigaïlov's patter, and then turns it into the most frightening scene since the murder itself. The patter is the trap. Every reassuring detail he gives Dounia on the way in (the porter who bows, the landlady next door, Sonia expected any minute) is inventory he will later read back to her as proof that no one can hear.

What I find remarkable is how much of the scene is argument. Svidrigaïlov summarises Raskolnikov's theory to his sister more coolly and more fairly than Raskolnikov ever managed in [[p5c4|his own confession]], and then shrugs it off in French: '_une théorie comme une autre_.' He is the one person in the book who is neither shocked by the idea nor impressed by it. And when he lays out why an assault could never be proved, he is doing exactly what Raskolnikov did in his garret: reasoning his way to a permission. The difference is that he knows it is sophistry and offers it to her as a courtesy, so that she 'need have no remorse.' I think that sentence is the vilest thing anyone says in the novel.

Then the revolver, and the scene stops being his. Dounia fires, grazes him, misfires, and at two paces, when she cannot miss, throws the gun down. She is the second Raskolnikov child to stand over a human being with the power to kill, and she finds out in a second what took her brother a book to learn. But the larger surprise is him. He wanted her to shoot or to love him; either would have been an answer. 'Never' is the one thing he had no plan for, and the man who has just explained that nobody could stop him hands over the key and tells her to hurry, because he does not trust himself for longer than that. It is the only moral act we see him perform that costs him anything, and he performs it with his back turned.

annotations.quote: The Schiller in you is in revolt every moment, and now you tell me not to listen at doors.
annotations.note: Schiller is Svidrigaïlov's shorthand for high-minded idealism, and the jab lands: a man who has taken an axe to two women is objecting to eavesdropping. It is a joke, but it is also the most accurate diagnosis of Raskolnikov anyone gives. His conscience is intact everywhere except where he overruled it.

annotations.quote: If he had only turned round on his way he might have seen Svidrigaïlov get out not a hundred paces off
annotations.note: The narrator steps outside Raskolnikov's head, which he almost never does, to show us what the hero misses. From here the chapter belongs to other people, and Raskolnikov, lost in thought on a bridge, walks straight past his own sister.

annotations.quote: The town is not the country. And even in the country you did me more harm than I did you.
annotations.note: He means it. In his own account he is the injured party of the affair on the estate, and that is what makes him persuasive: he never sounds like a man who thinks he is lying.

annotations.quote: It’s all right as a theory, _une théorie comme une autre_.
annotations.note: 'A theory like any other.' The idea that tore Raskolnikov apart is waved off as one opinion among many by a man who has never needed a theory to do what he liked. Nothing Porfiry said was as deflating.

annotations.quote: But it’s a misfortune to be broad without a special genius.
annotations.note: Slipped in as small talk, this is a verdict on Raskolnikov and on the speaker too. 'Broad' is the Russian breadth of nature that can hold the highest and lowest at once; without a gift to give it shape, he says, it is only chaos. He is describing himself and knows it.

annotations.quote: It is very difficult to prove an assault, Avdotya Romanovna.
annotations.note: The whole menace of the scene is in that polite use of her name and patronymic. He lays out the legal position like a solicitor, having counted the locked rooms beforehand.

annotations.quote: It was the deliverance from another feeling, darker and more bitter, which he could not himself have defined.
annotations.note: Dostoevsky declines to name it, and I think rightly. My guess is that some part of him was hoping she would do it, and the relief is at finding she is not someone who can kill; but the sentence is built to stay open.

annotations.quote: But there seemed a terrible significance in the tone of that “make haste.”
annotations.note: He is warning her against himself. The decency has a time limit and he knows roughly how many seconds it is good for.

annotations.quote: He thought a little, put the revolver in his pocket, took his hat and went out.
annotations.note: Four plain verbs. Notice that the narrator has just counted the charges left in the gun for us. Hold on to that.

links.why: The mother's letter, where we first heard of Dounia in Svidrigaïlov's house; this locked room is what that letter was afraid of.
The confession Svidrigaïlov overheard from his chair by the door, which he now retells in his own cooler words.
Raskolnikov with the axe raised and Dounia with the revolver raised: the same family at the same threshold, with opposite outcomes.

p6c6.essay:
This is the chapter I would hand to anyone who thinks Dostoevsky is all shouting. Hardly anyone raises a voice in it. A man gives away his money, takes a room, sleeps badly and goes out at dawn, and it is the most frightening thing in the book.

Start with how funny it is, because the comedy is deliberate. Svidrigaïlov spends his last evening arbitrating a dispute about a stolen teaspoon between clerks he likes because their noses bend in opposite directions. His fiancée's mother explains away a drenched midnight visitor by observing that 'Englishmen, for instance, are even more eccentric.' The waiter at the Adrianople is 'completely disillusioned' that a gentleman arriving at that hour wants only tea and veal. Dostoevsky keeps the world obstinately ordinary and a little ridiculous around him, and that is what a mind looks like when it has already left: everything is equally interesting and nothing matters. Meanwhile he puts his affairs in order with real precision. The orphans are provided for, with receipts. Sonia gets three thousand roubles and, more remarkably, an exact forecast of what she will need it for. He sees Raskolnikov's future more clearly than Raskolnikov does and quietly pays for it. I do not think the novel wants us to forgive him on this account, but it will not let us file him away as a monster either. The narrator warned us a chapter ago that Raskolnikov's verdict of 'coarse brute' was 'uttered too lightly.'

Then the room. Look at what he is given: low ceiling, one window, a sloping wall, wallpaper so worn that only the colour, yellow, can be made out. It is Raskolnikov's garret again, the yellow of every sickroom in this novel, and through a crack in the wall he watches a drunk lecturing another drunk, a little puppet show of the scenes we have sat through since [[p1c2|Marmeladov's tavern]]. He turns away 'indifferently.' Back in [[p4c1]] he proposed that eternity might be a small room like a country bath-house with spiders in the corners. He has checked into it.

The three dreams are the heart of the thing, and they come in an order. First the mouse, pure physical revulsion, running under his shirt. Then the flowers: a holiday, narcissus, cool air, a paragraph of real loveliness that walks him upstairs to a coffin, with a drowned girl of fourteen in it. The narrator never says in so many words that he was the cause. It does not need to; 'Svidrigaïlov knew that girl' is enough, and the rumours Luzhin retailed in [[p4c2]] stop being rumours. The third dream is the cruellest. He does a kind thing, undresses and warms a soaked five-year-old and tucks her in, and under his eyes the sleeping face turns knowing and inviting. This is the one moment in the book when Svidrigaïlov is horrified, 'in genuine horror,' and what horrifies him is his own imagination. He cannot even perform an act of pity without his mind corrupting its object. I read that as the real sentence passed on him, and he is the one who passes it. Dounia's 'never' closed the last door out; the dream shows him what he is shut in with.

Notice also who does not come. He lies in the dark and invites his wife's ghost, 'now is the time for you to turn up,' and gets nothing. The apparitions that visited him when he was comfortable desert him now. So does the storm he walked through; by morning there is only 'a thick milky mist.' He is a man who dislikes water 'even in a landscape' and spends his last night soaked, by a flooding river, planning a wet bush in a park, and then cannot be bothered to walk that far.

The ending is done almost entirely in the negative. He tries to catch a fly and fails. He settles for the nearest spot with 'an official witness,' a sleepy watchman in a fireman's helmet whom the narrator calls Achilles, and their exchange is a quarrel about whether this is 'the place.' The word he uses for what he is about to do is the one he has been using all week: America. He offered Raskolnikov the fare there yesterday. In this book America is where you go when you have decided there is nothing further to be said to anyone here. The chapter stops on a verb and gives us nothing after it, no sound, no body, no comment. Dostoevsky, who explains everything, explains nothing here, and I think the restraint is the measure of his respect for what he has made. Svidrigaïlov is the proof of where the idea that all is permitted comes out when a man holds it without fuss, without a theory and without anyone to love him. Raskolnikov spent this same night walking by the same river.

annotations.quote: Why, be starting for America, and be stopped by rain!
annotations.note: By now 'America' is a private code, and Sonia half hears it. The joke is very like him: he takes a real pleasure in saying exactly what he means in a form no one can answer.

annotations.quote: so torn and dusty that the pattern was indistinguishable, though the general colour--yellow--could still be made out.
annotations.note: Yellow again: the pawnbroker's wallpaper, Raskolnikov's garret, Sonia's room. Garnett sets it off between dashes as if the narrator had to squint for it. The novel's two transgressors end up in versions of the same cramped yellow box.

annotations.quote: “I never have liked water,” he thought, “even in a landscape,”
annotations.note: A fastidious remark, almost a drawing-room one, from a man soaked to the skin beside a rising river. He notices himself still having preferences and finds it comic, 'like an animal that picks out a special place.'

annotations.quote: now is the time for you to turn up; it’s dark, and the very time and place for you. But now you won’t come!
annotations.note: In [[p4c1]] he told Raskolnikov that Marfa Petrovna's ghost visited him about trifles: a clock, a dress. Tonight, when he would welcome even that company, nothing comes. Whatever the ghosts were, they were at least evidence that something was still addressing him.

annotations.quote: I never had a great hatred for anyone, I never particularly desired to avenge myself even, and that’s a bad sign
annotations.note: One of the strangest self-diagnoses in fiction. He counts his lack of hatred against himself, as proof that nothing ever mattered enough. It is the opposite of Raskolnikov, who hates and loves at full pitch and is perhaps for that reason still salvageable.

annotations.quote: there was no holy image, no burning candle beside the coffin; no sound of prayers: the girl had drowned herself.
annotations.note: The missing icon and candle are how we learn the cause of death: a suicide was denied the rites. The sentence turns the garden of narcissus into a judgment, and the wet hair explains why he cannot stand the sound of water.

annotations.quote: “What, at five years old?” Svidrigaïlov muttered in genuine horror.
annotations.note: The word 'genuine' matters; we have had three chapters of his performed feelings. What appals him is not the child but the discovery that his own mind will do this to a child he was trying to help.

annotations.quote: He tried till he was tired, but could not catch it.
annotations.note: The last thing he attempts in life is to catch a fly on a plate of cold veal, and he fails. Dostoevsky has him notice the absurdity ('this interesting pursuit') and get up. No last thoughts, no speech.

annotations.quote: His face wore that perpetual look of peevish dejection, which is so sourly printed on all faces of Jewish race without exception.
annotations.note: An ugly sentence, and it should be called one. Dostoevsky's antisemitism is a matter of record and it surfaces here as a casual generalisation at the most solemn moment of the chapter. I would rather stop at it than read past it.

annotations.quote: When you are asked, you just say he was going, he said, to America.
annotations.note: His last request is for a witness to pass on a joke. Compare the trouble he took to have Sonia mention his name to Razumihin: he wants to be reported accurately, by people who will not understand.

links.why: His first long talk with Raskolnikov: the ghost of Marfa Petrovna, the 'journey' he may take, and eternity as a bath-house with spiders.
Luzhin's catalogue of rumours about Svidrigaïlov, which the dream of the coffin among flowers quietly confirms.
Raskolnikov's dream of the beaten mare, the other great dream in which a sleeper meets what he is capable of.
The afternoon's cynical stories about his young fiancée, which read very differently after this night.

p6c7.essay:
After the silence of Svidrigaïlov's morning, two farewells, and they are built to contradict each other. With his mother Raskolnikov is a child again: he kneels, kisses her feet, asks her to pray. An hour later with Dounia he is shouting that there was no crime. I do not think either scene is a pose. The chapter's point is that both are true on the same evening, and that he knows it: 'I haven't faith, but I have just been weeping in mother's arms... I don't know how it is, Dounia, I don't understand it.'

The scene with Pulcheria Alexandrovna is almost unbearable for what it leaves unsaid. She has decided to be the mother of a genius. She is reading his article 'for the third time,' the very article that set Porfiry on him in [[p3c5]], and has found in it the explanation of everything: learned people are like that. He takes it from her, feels for a second what any author of twenty-three feels at seeing himself in print, and throws it down. And yet she is not fooled. Under the chatter she has known since the first evening, 'simply from your eyes,' and when he asks whether she will love him whatever she hears, she answers the question he did not ask: where are you going, is it far? Each is protecting the other from a sentence neither will say.

With Dounia he has no one to protect, and the old theory comes out at full strength, because she uses the word 'crime.' I find this speech important to take seriously rather than explain away. He is on his way to give himself up and he has not changed his mind about anything. Blood 'is spilt like champagne' by men who get statues; his own failing was clumsiness; scruples about how a killing looks are 'the first symptom of impotence.' Then he meets her eyes and stops, not because he is refuted but because he has made 'these two poor women miserable.' That is the whole mechanism of the chapter. Nothing in his head will take him where he is going. What takes him is in the last paragraph, where he wishes that no one loved him, since then 'nothing of all this would have happened,' and asks for the hundredth time why he should go. Dostoevsky answers in four words and no reasons.

annotations.quote: that every author experiences the first time he sees himself in print; besides, he was only twenty-three.
annotations.note: A rare moment of tenderness from the narrator, and the only time I can recall being reminded of his exact age so pointedly. For one instant he is just a young writer with a first publication. Then he remembers what the article argued.

annotations.quote: And they dared to think you were mad!
annotations.note: She has taken the article as proof of sanity and greatness. The reader knows it as the document that made a detective look twice at him. Dostoevsky lets the irony stand without a word of comment.

annotations.quote: No, but kneel down and pray to God for me. Your prayer perhaps will reach Him.
annotations.note: 'Perhaps' and 'Your' carry the weight. He does not say God is not there; he says his own prayers would not arrive. It is the nearest thing to belief he has uttered, and it is put as doubt about himself.

annotations.quote: he seemed to be glad to think that he was still proud.
annotations.note: He has just called his refusal to drown himself pride, and Dounia echoes the word back. Whether she means it as praise or diagnosis, he hears praise. The thing that got him into this is the last thing he wants to lose.

annotations.quote: Killing her was atonement for forty sins.
annotations.note: A Russian proverbial turn: kill a spider and forty sins are forgiven. He reaches for folk wisdom to call the old woman vermin, the same arithmetic he overheard in the tavern in [[p1c6]], unchanged by everything since.

annotations.quote: The fear of appearances is the first symptom of impotence.
annotations.note: His answer to the objection that an axe is ugly and a siege is glorious. As an argument about hypocrisy it is not stupid, which is what makes the speech hard to dismiss. He is going to the police with his theory intact.

annotations.quote: It was the portrait of his landlady’s daughter, who had died of fever, that strange girl who had wanted to be a nun.
annotations.note: The dead fiancée, mentioned in passing in [[p3c3]] and almost forgotten. He says he told her 'much of what has since been so hideously realised,' so there was a first confidante before Sonia, also sickly and devout, and she argued against it too.

annotations.quote: Oh, if only I were alone and no one loved me and I too had never loved anyone!
annotations.note: The italicised sentence that follows it is the key: without these attachments nothing would have happened. I take that both ways. Love is what is forcing him to confess, and the wish to do something for those he loved was part of how he talked himself into the deed.

annotations.quote: It was the hundredth time perhaps that he had asked himself that question since the previous evening, but still he went.
annotations.note: A hundred questions and a body that keeps walking. The narrator gives no motive because there is none Raskolnikov could state. Compare the opposite condition before the murder, when his reasons were all in order and his legs carried him 'mechanically.'

links.why: Porfiry's dissection of the article 'On Crime' that the mother is now reading as proof of her son's greatness.
Her long letter at the start; set it beside this scene to see how much she has learned to leave unasked.
Porfiry's advice to confess and accept suffering, which Raskolnikov sneers at here as something done 'for my advantage.'

p6c8.essay:
Everything about the confession is slightly wrong, and that is why I believe it. A novelist with less nerve would have given us a penitent. Dostoevsky gives us a man who comes for a cross and makes a joke of it ('the symbol of my taking up the cross'), forgets to say goodbye, snaps at the one person who will follow him, and realises on the stairs that he went to her only because he 'wanted her tears.' He has not been converted. He has run out of other things to do.

The Hay Market is the centre of the chapter. Sonia told him in [[p5c4]] to bow down at the cross-roads and say aloud that he is a murderer, and for a moment he can do the first half. It comes 'like a fit,' a physical softening, and he kisses 'that filthy earth,' and the crowd decides he is drunk, or off to Jerusalem. The laughter is enough to stop the words in his throat. So the public confession the scene seems built for does not happen. The earth gets its bow; the people get nothing. I find that exact: he is capable of a gesture toward the ground he has wronged well before he is capable of facing anyone standing on it.

Then the police office, and Dostoevsky, at the climax of a six-part tragedy, writes a comic monologue. The Explosive Lieutenant, who bullied him over an IOU in [[p2c1]], has been told he is a literary man and will not stop being gracious: hats, Livingstone, nihilists, lady doctors he calls 'midwives.' Raskolnikov cannot get a word in to ruin his life. It is very funny and it is torture, and in the middle of the babble a name drops from the next room 'with drowsy listlessness.' The reader has known since the morning. He has not, and it nearly undoes him: the only other man who knew, and who showed him the other exit, has taken it. He says 'good-bye' and walks out. He is, for the length of a staircase, free.

What turns him is not a thought. It is Sonia standing in the yard with her hands clasped, saying nothing. He grins, 'an ugly, meaningless smile,' and goes back up. The sentence he finally speaks is the plainest in the book, set in italics, with the two victims named and the axe and the robbery, no theory anywhere in it. Then: 'Raskolnikov repeated his statement.' The novel proper ends on a clerk's phrase.

annotations.quote: she could see nothing but the unwhitewashed blank wall of the next house.
annotations.note: The view from Sonia's window while she waits to learn whether he is alive. This book rarely lets anyone see farther than the next building; remember that wall when the horizon finally opens.

annotations.quote: It was the green _drap de dames_ shawl of which Marmeladov had spoken, “the family shawl.”
annotations.note: From Marmeladov's tavern confession in [[p1c2]]: the shawl Sonia lay under, face to the wall, the night she first came home with thirty roubles. She puts it on now to follow a second man into his disgrace. Raskolnikov recognises it and says nothing.

annotations.quote: No, I wanted her tears, I wanted to see her terror, to see how her heart ached!
annotations.note: A ruthless piece of self-knowledge delivered on a staircase. He sees that he used her grief as something to hold on to. It is harsher than anything he has yet admitted about the murder.

annotations.quote: It’s written here ‘Campany,’ that’s a thing to remember, that letter _a_
annotations.note: A misspelt shop sign, and he tries to fix it in memory as a condemned man would. Garnett invents an English misspelling to match the Russian one. The mind going to trivia under extreme pressure is something Dostoevsky knew at first hand.

annotations.quote: kissed that filthy earth with bliss and rapture.
annotations.note: 'Filthy' is the honest word. This is the Hay Market, the dirtiest square in the city, not a symbolic Russian soil. The rapture is real and lasts until someone speaks.

annotations.quote: He’s bowing down to all the world and kissing the great city of St. Petersburg and its pavement
annotations.note: The workman is mocking, and he is also, without knowing it, describing precisely what is happening. The crowd is right in every detail and misses the whole.

annotations.quote: Dostoevsky appears to have forgotten that it is after sunset
annotations.note: Garnett's own footnote, catching the author in a slip of timekeeping. I am fond of it. A translator stepping in to say the great man nodded is a reminder that this was written fast, in instalments, for money.

annotations.quote: As for a hat--well, what does a hat matter?
annotations.note: On the first page of the novel Raskolnikov was terrified that his conspicuous hat would give him away. The officer now assures him, at the worst possible moment, that hats are nothing and what is under them is everything.

annotations.quote: “Svidrigaïlov,” someone answered from the other room with drowsy listlessness.
annotations.note: The whole of the previous chapter reduced to a bored clerk supplying a surname. This is how the news reaches the one man it concerns most, and the reader watches it land.

annotations.quote: His lips worked in an ugly, meaningless smile.
annotations.note: No softening, no resolve on his face, just a grimace, and then he turns round. Dostoevsky refuses to make the decisive moment handsome. Sonia does not speak or beckon; her being there is the whole argument.

links.why: Sonia's command to go to the cross-roads and her first offer of the cypress cross, which he refused then.
His first visit to this office, the same stairs and stench, the same lieutenant, and the faint that started the suspicion.
Marmeladov's account of the green shawl and of the day Sonia first went out.
The death that is reported here in one drowsy word, as it actually happened.

ep1.essay:
The voice changes at once. 'Siberia.' A one-word sentence, then a river, a town, a fortress, a prison, each inside the last like nested boxes, and for the first time in the book we are not inside Raskolnikov's fever. This chapter is a report, most of it at second hand, and I think it is among the best things in the novel precisely because it is so dry.

The trial is quiet satire. The court cannot believe a man would rob and never count the money, so the lawyers 'more versed in psychology' reach for the fashionable theory of temporary insanity, and the thing that saves him is the very carelessness that proves how little the robbery ever mattered. Raskolnikov will not help them. Asked for his motive he says poverty and three thousand roubles; asked why he confessed he says 'heartfelt repentance.' The narrator's comment, twice, is that this was 'almost coarse.' Having just read [[p6c7]] we know why: it is a lie told in the bluntest available words, by a man who will not expose his real idea to a courtroom. And then Razumihin turns up the consumptive student and the children pulled from a fire. Dostoevsky slips in after six hundred pages that his murderer has also been, unobserved, something like a hero. It is late and almost offhand, and it disturbs the picture more than any speech.

The mother's story is the part I find hardest to read. She never asks where he is. She builds a version with powerful enemies and a brilliant career, sleeps with the article, stops strangers in shops to tell them about the fire, and then one morning starts cleaning the room for his return. It is denial drawn with complete sympathy, and the last clause about what she let slip in delirium turns it into something braver: she knew, and she carried it alone so the others could believe she did not.

Then Sonia's letters, which Dounia and Razumihin first find 'dry and unsatisfactory.' No hopes, no interpretation, only what he said, what he ate, how he looked. After a novel in which everyone has theorised about Raskolnikov's soul, including Raskolnikov, the person who loves him most declines to. What the facts show is a man gone inert: not rebellious, not penitent, merely absent. The chapter ends with him in hospital and no explanation offered.

annotations.quote: in the town there is a fortress, in the fortress there is a prison.
annotations.note: The syntax narrows like a funnel. Dostoevsky served four years in the fortress prison at Omsk, on the Irtish, and the unnamed town is his. After Petersburg's crowds the plainness is almost a relief.

annotations.quote: There turned out to be in the purse three hundred and seventeen roubles and sixty copecks.
annotations.note: We finally learn what two lives were worth in cash, to the copeck, and learn it before he does. The top notes have rotted under the stone from [[p2c2]]. The exactness is the court's, and it mocks the grand arithmetic of the theory.

annotations.quote: To the question what led him to confess, he answered that it was his heartfelt repentance.
annotations.note: The stock answer, given flatly. Set it beside his outburst to Dounia a few hours before he confessed and it is plain he is handing the court the formula it wants in order to be left alone.

annotations.quote: Raskolnikov had rescued two little children from a house on fire and was burnt in doing so.
annotations.note: A startling thing to be told now. The same impulsiveness that we saw give away his last roubles had, before the book began, sent him into a burning house. Dostoevsky holds it back so that it can never work as an excuse, only as a complication.

annotations.quote: This article she was continually reading, she even read it aloud, almost took it to bed with her
annotations.note: The essay that argued some men may step over blood has become a mother's relic. She cannot understand it and it is all she has of him. I can think of few crueller ironies in the book, or gentler ones.

annotations.quote: she knew a great deal more about her son’s terrible fate than they had supposed.
annotations.note: One sentence, after her death, revises everything we were told about her. The fantasies were partly a shield for Dounia's sake. It matches her last scene with him, where she understood and did not ask.

annotations.quote: There could be no mistake, because nothing was given but facts.
annotations.note: I read this as a small manifesto. Sonia's method is the opposite of the novel's and of its hero's: no psychology, no hypothesis. And the picture comes out 'with great clearness.'

annotations.quote: not from any plan or design, but simply from inattention and indifference.
annotations.note: In Petersburg his squalor was half a statement. Here even that is gone. He is not mortifying himself; he has simply stopped attending to his own life, which is more alarming than any defiance.

links.why: His farewell to his mother and his 'What crime?' to Dounia, the background to both her illness and his answers in court.
The stone in the yard where he buried the purse unopened, now produced in evidence.
Porfiry's promise of a lighter sentence for a voluntary confession; the narrator notes he 'fully kept his word.'

ep2.essay:
The last chapter has been argued over ever since it was published. One camp calls it a pious appendix, a conversion the novel has not earned; the other says the whole book was built toward it from the Lazarus reading in [[p4c4]]. I have been in both camps at different readings. Where I have come to rest is that most of this chapter is as hard and truthful as anything before it, that the turn itself is too thinly written, and that Dostoevsky half admits as much in his final paragraph.

Take the first half, which complaints about a sentimental ending tend to skip. Nine months into Siberia, 'he did not repent of his crime.' He would be glad to; 'tears and agonies would at least have been life.' What he feels instead is shame at having bungled, and the phrase the narrator italicises for prison is '_in freedom_': here, with nothing to hide and no one to deceive, he reviews the theory at leisure and finds it no worse than any other. It is success that makes right; he failed; that is all. I admire Dostoevsky for this. He lets the idea survive confession, trial and hard labour, because an idea like that is not dislodged by consequences. The narrator can say that there was a 'fundamental falsity' he was 'dimly conscious' of at the river, but he says it over Raskolnikov's head, as something the man 'didn't understand.'

Two things work on him, and neither is an argument. The first is the other convicts. They value life in a way that amazes him: a tramp remembering a cold spring in the forest as he would a sweetheart. They hate him without knowing why, try to kill him as an infidel though he has never spoken of God, and tell him an axe is 'not a gentleman's work.' And they love Sonia, for no reason he can isolate. The murderer who divided mankind into the extraordinary and the lice finds himself the only one in the barracks who is nobody's brother. The theory required him to stand apart; now he has what it required.

The second is the dream of the plague, which I think is the greatest page in the Epilogue and one of the great prophetic passages of the century. Microbes 'endowed with intelligence and will' infect men with certainty. Each is sure 'that he alone had the truth'; they cannot agree what is good or evil; armies dissolve on the march; the alarm bell rings and nobody knows who rang it. It is his own idea, one man entitled to judge alone, multiplied by the population of the earth. No one refutes him. He is shown what the world looks like when everyone is Raskolnikov, and it 'haunted his memory so miserably' without his knowing why. That is exactly how this novel has always changed him: through dreams and the body, never through debate. The mare in [[p1c5]] told him what the murder was before he did it; the plague tells him what the theory was after.

Then the riverbank. A wide empty river, singing from the far side, the nomads' tents, time standing still 'as though the age of Abraham and his flocks had not passed.' After six parts in stairwells and yellow rooms the book finally has a horizon, and I feel the release every time. Sonia sits down beside him. And then: 'How it happened he did not know. But all at once something seemed to seize him and fling him at her feet.'

This is where I hesitate. Structurally it is right. Everything decisive he has done was done this way, seized rather than decided, and it is consistent that love arrives as the murder did, from below thought. 'Life had stepped into the place of theory' is the truest sentence in the chapter. But the prose around it goes soft. 'Infinite happiness,' 'a full resurrection into a new life,' 'he had risen again and he knew it': the narrator is telling me in the vocabulary of a sermon what the novel has until now always made me watch. And 'she only lived in his life' troubles me. Sonia has been the strongest person in the book; she deserves a better clause.

What keeps me from dismissing the ending is how much Dostoevsky withholds. Raskolnikov does not open the Testament under his pillow. He does not pray. He never, on the page, says that the killing was wrong. His one thought is a question: 'Can her convictions not be mine now?' Seven years remain, and we are told the new life 'would cost him great striving.' The last paragraph calls all that 'a new story.' I take him at his word. He knew the regeneration could not be written in six pages, wrote the first hour of it, and stopped. The result is a little too bright and far too brief, but it does not claim more than a beginning.

annotations.quote: Oh, how happy he would have been if he could have blamed himself!
annotations.note: The Epilogue's first surprise. We expect a penitent in chains; we get a man who would welcome guilt as a relief and cannot find any. His conscience has examined the murder and returned a verdict of blunder.

annotations.quote: But now in prison, _in freedom_, he thought over and criticised all his actions again
annotations.note: The italics are a deliberate paradox. In Petersburg he was hunted and feverish; here nothing more can happen to him and he can think coolly. And thinking coolly, he acquits himself. It is the bleakest moment in the book.

annotations.quote: But those men succeeded and so _they were right_, and I didn’t
annotations.note: The theory stripped to its core: right is what wins. It is the Napoleon argument from [[p3c5]] with the idealism burned off. A year and a half on, this is still what he believes.

annotations.quote: You shouldn’t hack about with an axe; that’s not a gentleman’s work.
annotations.note: The convicts' objection is not moral but social, and it stings more. To them he is a gentleman playing at their trade. Dostoevsky met this same wall between educated prisoners and peasants in his own four years of hard labour.

annotations.quote: Each thought that he alone had the truth and was wretched looking at the others
annotations.note: The sentence I would underline in the dream. The infected are not gleeful; they are miserable, beating their breasts over everyone else's error. It is a precise picture of where the right to judge alone leads, and it has not dated.

annotations.quote: as though the age of Abraham and his flocks had not passed.
annotations.note: The first long view in the novel. Across the river is a life before theories, before Petersburg, before history. Abraham is also the man called out of his country to begin again, which is quietly to the point.

annotations.quote: How it happened he did not know.
annotations.note: The honest sentence, and the disputed one. The novel has prepared us for a change that comes without reasons, since everything he does comes that way. Whether a change so large can be passed over in six words is the question the whole Epilogue turns on.

annotations.quote: while she--she only lived in his life.
annotations.note: The clause I like least in the book. After hundreds of pages in which Sonia outlasts everyone, her happiness is defined as a part of his. It reads as the narrator's piety rather than as anything we have seen of her.

annotations.quote: Life had stepped into the place of theory and something quite different would work itself out in his mind.
annotations.note: If one sentence states what the novel believes, it is this. The idea is not refuted; it is displaced. Note the future tense, 'would work itself out': the thinking has not been done yet.

annotations.quote: That might be the subject of a new story, but our present story is ended.
annotations.note: Dostoevsky draws the line himself. I read it as modesty and as a concession: the renewal of a man is a different, slower book, and he never wrote it. What we have been given is the crime, the punishment, and one morning.

links.why: Sonia reading the raising of Lazarus from this same New Testament; the unopened book under his pillow points back here.
The dream of the beaten mare, the novel's first great dream; the plague is its counterpart at the other end.
The theory of extraordinary men as he first defended it to Porfiry, which he is still defending to himself in prison.
The confession that ended the novel proper without a word of repentance, the gap the Epilogue is trying to cross.
